summary: A local news feature on how young people in the city are driving conservation and sustainability. It covers school programs, an eco app, policy advocacy, community clean-ups, native plant gardens, classroom changes, and a mural project. The piece argues that youth are influencing peers, adults, businesses and policymakers toward an eco-friendly community culture.
one_line: Local youth-led conservation efforts, from school recycling and an eco app to policy advocacy, gardens and murals, are shaping the city's sustainability culture.
key_facts: Maple High School's 'Green Ambassadors' program launched on September 12th, 2023, led by 17-year-old Jordan Harris, and set up recycling and composting systems replacing a single trash-bin policy.
The Green Ambassadors run a monthly green market selling organic produce grown in the school's new urban garden.

Lincoln Tech Academy students created the 'EcoChallenge App', unveiled at a school assembly on October 5th, 2023, which tracks carbon footprints, promotes local clean-ups and offers gamified challenges and rewards.
Local businesses offer discounts and deals to EcoChallenge App users who reach eco-friendly goals; Sara Nguyen, 16, is a developer of the app.
A student delegation met with city officials on November 22nd after student-led demonstrations in fall 2023, presenting a student-drafted proposal to reduce the city's carbon emissions.
Roberta Clark, an 18-year-old climate advocate, spearheaded the student delegation to city officials.
On September 30th, children and parents joined a community clean-up at Echo Park organized by 'Kid's Earth Club', a non-profit founded by 12-year-old Mia Peterson and friends.
Kid's Earth Club also runs regular workshops on recycling, composting and wildlife.

'Roots of Tomorrow', launched October 15th by high school juniors Zoe Ramirez, Lucas Smith and Ayesha Khan, turns empty lots into wildflower gardens and partners with ecologists to pick plants suited to the local climate.

Several schools in the district have integrated environmental science modules and project-based learning this school year; Ms. Linda Jackson of Sunnyside Elementary has set up bird watching clubs and tree planting days.
The 'Murals for Mother Earth' project, begun November 2nd and led by 15-year-old Emma Torres, is a city-sanctioned initiative using alleyways and building walls for conservation-themed art.
